newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: PAKISTAN SEEKS NEW POWERS TO QUELL VIOLENCE.
newsitem.headline: PAKISTAN SEEKS NEW POWERS TO QUELL VIOLENCE.

text.p: The Pakistani government presented a bill in the National Assembly (lower house) on Wednesday that would give it sweeping new security powers.
The controversial legislation is an attempt to stop a wave of killings that has shaken Pakistan in the run-up to Thursday's golden jubilee celebration of 50 years of independence.

More than 225 people have been killed in a feud involving rival wings of an ethnic party in Karachi so far this year, while a vendetta between militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem factions has cost about 140 lives, mostly in Punjab province.

"There is a spate of terrorist activities and commission of heinous offences in Pakistan," said the draft law proposed by Interior Minister Shujaat Hussain. "It is necessary that appropriate administrative and judicial measures are adopted."

The legislation, virtually certain to pass thanks to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's commanding majority in both houses of parliament, would let the federal or provincial governments call in the armed forces to help civilian authorities.
It would authorise policemen, or soldiers deployed in such cases, to fire on anyone committing or believed to be about to commit a "terrorist" offence.

The security forces would also be allowed to arrest terrorist suspects without a warrant and to search any premises and seize weapons or anything else used or likely to be used in a terrorist offence, again without a warrant.
The draft bill proposed the death penalty for any terrorist whose action has resulted in a death, and a sentence of between seven years and life imprisonment otherwise.
It would ban "acts intended or likely to stir up sectarian hatred" and punish their perpetrators with sentences of up to seven years of rigorous imprisonment.

The bill would enable the government to set up special courts, with police required to complete investigation of cases within seven working days. The courts would have to decide such cases within a further seven days with a similar period for an appellate tribunal to judge appeals against their verdicts.
The federal or provincial governments could declare any association unlawful "in the interest of public order".
Sharif's government has come under intense pressure to halt the bloodletting in Karachi and Punjab, with many newspaper commentators calling for sectarian groups to be banned.
